readings.c2s2:
¶

Also spelled ''vocalise.''

'''vocally''' (vō′kạl-i), ''adv.'' '''1.''' In a vocal manner; with voice.—'''2.''' In words; verbally; orally.
{{smaller block|To express . . . desires ''vocally.''
{{right|''Sir M. Hale,'' Origin of Mankind.}}}}
'''3.''' In song; by means of singing: opposed to ''instrumentally.''—'''4.''' In respect of vowels or vocalic sounds.
{{smaller block|Syllables which are ''vocally'' of the lowest consideration.
{{right|''Earle,'' Philology of Eng. Tongue, xii. § 647.}}}}

'''vocalness''' (vō′kạl-nes), ''n.'' The quality of being vocal; vocality.

'''vocation''' (vọ̄-kā′shọn), ''n.'' [< F. ''vocation'' = Sp. ''vocacion'' = Pg. ''vocação'' = It. ''vocazione,'' < L. ''vocatio(n-),'' a summons, a calling, < ''vocare,'' pp. ''vocatus,'' call, < ''vox'' (''voc-''), voice: see ''voice.''] '''1.''' A calling or designation to a particular activity, office, or duty; a summons; a call; in ''theol.,'' a call, under God’s guidance, to the Christian life or some special state, service, or ministry.
{{smaller block|Follow thou thy ''vocation,'' and serve the king when he calleth thee. ''Latimer,'' 2d Sermon bef. Edw. VI., 1550.

Heaven is his ''vocation,'' and therefore he counts earthly employments avocations.
{{right|''Fuller,'' Holy and Profane State, IV. ix. 10.}}

The golden chain of ''vocation,'' election, and justification.
{{right|''Jer. Taylor.''}}

Where there is the perception of an ideal, we may expect to find the sense of a ''vocation.''
{{right|''J. R. Seeley,'' Nat. Religion, p. 127.}}}}
'''2.''' Employment; occupation; avocation; calling; business; trade: including professions as well as mechanical occupations. See ''avocation,'' 5.

'''Vochysia''' (vō-kis′i-ä̤), ''n.'' [NL. (Jussieu, 1789), from the name among the Galibis of Guiana.] A genus of plants, type of the order ''Vochysiaceæ.''
{{smaller block|It is characterized by flowers with three (or fewer) petals, a single fertile stamen, and a three-celled ovary with two ovules in each cell. There are about 55 species, natives of Brazil, Guiana, eastern Peru, and the United States of Colombia. They are tall trees, or sometimes shrubs, often resinous, and with very handsomely netted-veined coriaceous leaves. The flowers are large, bright-orange or yellow, and odorous, forming elongated compound racemes or panicles; the leaves are decussate and opposite, or whorled. The wood is a valuable compact but not durable timber; that of ''V. Guianensis'' is known as ''itaballi-wood'' and ''copaiyé-wood.'' The flowers are singularly irregular: the posterior sepal is much larger than the other four, and usually spurred, and the petals are linear and spatulate, the anterior being much the larger. The fruit is a coriaceous and woody three-celled and three-valved capsule, containing three erect winged or cottony seeds.}}

readings.c3s4:
¶
'''vociferator''' (vọ̄-sif′e̤-rā-to̤r), ''n.'' One who vociferates; a clamorous shouter.
{{smaller block|He defied the ''vociferators'' to do their worst.
{{right|''Daily Telegraph'', Oct. 27, 1887. (''Encyc. Dict.'')}}}}

'''vociferize''' (vọ̄-sif′ėr-īz), ''v.'' Same as ''vociferate.'' [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Let the singing singers
With vocal voices, most vociferous
In sweet vociferation, out-''vociferize''
Even sound itself.</poem>
{{right|''Carey'', Chrononhotonthologos, i. 1.}}}}

'''vociferosity''' (vọ̄-sif-e̤-ros′ị-ti), ''n.'' [< ''vociferous'' + ''-ity.''] The character of being vociferous; vociferation; clamorousness. [Rare.]

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|vocal|6779|vociferosity}}</noinclude>{{nop}}{{smaller block|Some years hence, for all we know, we may be able to transmit the ''vocal'' message itself, with the very inflection, tone, and accent of the speaker.
{{right|''J. Baille'' (1871), quoted in Prescott’s Elect. Invent., p. 47.}}}}

{{smaller block|A tin pipe ascends through the ceiling, and forms a medium of ''vocal'' communication with other parts of the edifice.
{{right|''Hawthorne'', Scarlet Letter, Int., p. 7.}}}}

'''2.''' Having a voice; endowed, or as if endowed, with a voice; possessed of utterance or audible expression.
{{smaller block|<poem>The stream, the wood, the gale,
Is ''vocal'' with the plaintive wail.</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', L. of L. M., v. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The roving bee proclaims aloud
Her flight by ''vocal'' wings.</poem>
{{right|''Wordsworth'', Gold and Silver Fishes in a Vase.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The tide flows down, the wave again
Is ''vocal'' in its wooded walls.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', In Memoriam, xix.}}}}
'''3.''' In ''phonetics:'' (''a'') Voiced; uttered with voice as distinct from breath; sonant: said of certain alphabetic sounds or letters, as ''z'' or ''v'' or ''b'' as distinguished from ''s'' or ''f'' or ''p'' respectively. (''b'') Having a vowel character or function; vowel.
{{smaller block|The ''vocal'' (vowel) mechanism is the first that is manifested in the child.
{{right|''Alien. and Neurol.'' (trans.), VIII. 7.}}}}

'''4.''' In ''zoöl.'', voiced; uttered by the mouth; formed in the vocal organs: distinguished from ''sonorific'': noting the cries of animals, as distinguished from the mechanical noises they may make, as the stridulation of an insect.—{{smaller|'''Vocal auscultation''', examination by the sound of the voice as transmitted through the lungs and chest-wall.—'''Vocal cords.''' See ''cord''<sup>1</sup>.—'''Vocal fremitus''', a vibration felt on palpation of the wall of the chest when the subject speaks in an audible tone. Also called ''voice-thrill'', ''pectoral fremitus'', and ''pectoral thrill''.—'''Vocal glottis.''' Same as ''rima vocalis'' (which see, under ''rima'').—'''Vocal music''', music prepared for or produced by the human voice alone or accompanied by instruments, in distinction from ''instrumental music'', which is prepared for or produced by instruments alone.—'''Vocal process''', the prolonged inner basal angle of the arytenoid cartilage, to which the true vocal cord is attached.—'''Vocal resonance.''' See ''resonance''.—'''Vocal score.''' See ''score''<sup>1</sup>, 9.—'''Vocal spiracle''', in ''entom.'', a thoracic spiracle or breathing-pore having a peculiar interior apparatus supposed to produce sounds, as in the bees and many flies.—'''Vocal tone''', an instrumental tone similar in quality to the singing-tone of the human voice.—'''Vocal tube''', in ''anat.'', the space which the sound of the voice has to traverse after it is produced in the glottis, including the passages through the nose and mouth.}}

'''II.''' ''n.'' In the ''Rom. Cath. Ch.'', a man who has a right to vote in certain elections.

'''vocalic''' (vō-kal′ik), ''a.''   [< ''vocal'' + ''-ic''.]   Relating to, consisting of, or resembling vowel sounds; containing many vowels.
{{smaller block|The Gaelic language, being uncommonly ''vocalic'', is well adapted for sudden and extemporaneous poetry.
{{right|''Scott'', Waverley, xxii.}}}}
{{smaller block|The vowels become more consonantal; the consonants become more ''vocalic''.
{{right|''Whitney'', Life and Growth of Lang., iv.}}}}

'''vocalisation, vocalise.''' See ''vocalization, vocalize.''

'''vocalism''' (vō′kạl-izm), ''n.''   [< F. ''vocalisme''; as ''vocal'' + ''-ism.'']   '''1.''' The exercise of the vocal organs in speech or song; vocalization.
{{smaller block|We should now be talking in monosyllables, and eking out our scantiness of ''vocalism'' by nods, shrugs, winks, and other resources of pantomime.
{{right|''F. Hall,'' Mod. Eng., p. 19.}}}}
'''2.''' A vocalic sound.
{{smaller block|To utter such thick-lipped ''vocalisms'' as Mosos.
{{right|''Earle,'' Philology of Eng. Tongue, i. § 126.}}}}
'''3.''' See ''nominalism.''

'''vocalist''' (vō′kạl-ist), ''n.''   [< F. ''vocaliste''; as ''vocal'' + ''-ist.'']   A vocal musician; a singer, as opposed to an instrumental performer.
{{smaller block|She was a good ''vocalist''; and, even in speech, her voice commanded a great range of changes.
{{right|''R. L. Stevenson,'' Prince Otto, ii. 4.}}}}

'''vocality''' (vō-kal′i-ti), ''n.''; pl. ''vocalities'' (-tiz).   [= Sp. ''vocalidad,'' < L. ''vocalita(t-)s'' (tr. Gr. εὐφωνία), open sound, euphony, < ''vocalis,'' sounding, sonorous: see ''vocal.'']   The quality of being vocal. {{smaller|(''a'') The quality of being utterable or capable of being expressed by the voice in speech or song.}}
{{smaller block|I did hear Mrs. Manuel and one of the Italians, her gallant, sing well. But yet I confess I am not delighted so much with it as to admire it; for not understanding the words, I lose the benefit of the ''vocalitys'' of the musick, and it proves only instrumental.
{{right|''Pepys,'' Diary, III. 334.}}}}

{{smaller block|L and R being in extreams, one of Roughness, the other of Smoothness and freeness of ''Vocality'', are not easie, in tract of Vocal speech, to be pronounced spiritally.
{{right|''Holder'', Elem. of Speech, p. 58.}}}}

{{smaller|(''b'') The quality of being a vowel; vowel character: as, the ''vocality'' of a sound.}}

'''vocalization''' (vō″kal-i-zā′shon), ''n.''   [< F. ''vocalisation'' = Sp. ''vocalizacion''; as ''vocalize'' + ''-ation''.]   '''1.''' The act of vocalizing or uttering with the voice, the state of being so uttered, or the manner of such utterance, whether in speech or in song: as, the deceptive ''vocalizations'' of a ventriloquist.
{{smaller block|Knowing what one discontented woman can do in the way of ''vocalization'', it is possible to imagine the clamor multiplied by hundreds.
{{right|''The Century'', XXXVII. 585.}}}}
'''2.''' The formation and utterance of vowel sounds.
{{smaller block|''Vocalization'' (vowelizing) is the expression of an emotion, an indistinct sensation, not an idea.
{{right|''Alien. and Neurol.'' (trans.), VIII. 7.}}}}
Also spelled ''vocalisation.''

'''vocalize''' (vō′kạl-īz), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''vocalized'', ppr. ''vocalizing.''   [< F. ''vocaliser'' = Sp. ''vocalizar'' = It. ''vocalizzare''; as ''vocal'' + ''-ize.'']   '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To form into voice; make vocal.
{{smaller block|It is one thing to breath, or give impulse to breath alone, and another thing to ''vocalize'' that breath, i. e., in its passage through the larynx to give it the sound of humane voyce.
{{right|''Holder'', Elem. of Speech, p. 30.}}}}
'''2.''' To utter with voice and not merely with breath; make sonant: as, ''f vocalized'' is equivalent to ''v.''—'''3.''' To write with vowel points; insert the vowels in, as in the writing of the Semitic languages.
{{smaller block|The question “Should Turkish poetry be ''vocalized?''” is answered in the affirmative by R. Dvorak. Arabic books, especially Arabic poetry, are ''vocalized'' in the East as well as in the West. Turkish books to some extent, and this should be done throughout. D. advocates the use of Arabic vowel-signs, which would prove a great help to the student.
{{right|''Amer. Jour. Philol.'', X. 232.}}}}
'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To use the voice; speak; sing; hum.
{{smaller block|The young lady who was still strolling along in front of them, softly ''vocalizing''.
{{right|''H. James, Jr.'', Daisy Miller, i. 45.}}}}

Also spelled ''vocalise.''

'''vocally''' (vō′kạl-i), ''adv.'' '''1.''' In a vocal manner; with voice.—'''2.''' In words; verbally; orally.
{{smaller block|To express . . . desires ''vocally.''
{{right|''Sir M. Hale,'' Origin of Mankind.}}}}
'''3.''' In song; by means of singing: opposed to ''instrumentally.''—'''4.''' In respect of vowels or vocalic sounds.
{{smaller block|Syllables which are ''vocally'' of the lowest consideration.
{{right|''Earle,'' Philology of Eng. Tongue, xii. § 647.}}}}

'''vocalness''' (vō′kạl-nes), ''n.'' The quality of being vocal; vocality.

'''vocation''' (vọ̄-kā′shọn), ''n.''   [< F. ''vocation'' = Sp. ''vocacion'' = Pg. ''vocação'' = It. ''vocazione,'' < L. ''vocatio(n-),'' a summons, a calling, < ''vocare,'' pp. ''vocatus,'' call, < ''vox'' (''voc-''), voice: see ''voice.'']   '''1.''' A calling or designation to a particular activity, office, or duty; a summons; a call; in ''theol.,'' a call, under God’s guidance, to the Christian life or some special state, service, or ministry.
{{smaller block|Follow thou thy ''vocation,'' and serve the king when he calleth thee. ''Latimer,'' 2d Sermon bef. Edw. VI., 1550.

Heaven is his ''vocation,'' and therefore he counts earthly employments avocations.
{{right|''Fuller,'' Holy and Profane State, IV. ix. 10.}}}}
{{smaller block|The golden chain of ''vocation,'' election, and justification.
{{right|''Jer. Taylor.''}}}}
{{smaller block|Where there is the perception of an ideal, we may expect to find the sense of a ''vocation.''
{{right|''J. R. Seeley,'' Nat. Religion, p. 127.}}}}
'''2.''' Employment; occupation; avocation; calling; business; trade: including professions as well as mechanical occupations. See ''avocation,'' 5.

{{smaller block|Why, Hal, ’tis my ''vocation'', Hal; ’tis no sin for a man to labour in his ''vocation''. {{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. IV., i. 2. 116.}}}}
{{smaller block|The respective or special duty of every man, in his profession, ''vocation'', and place.
{{right|''Bacon'', Advancement of Learning, ii.}}}}
{{smaller block|If wit or wisdom be the head, if honesty be the heart, industry is the right hand of every ''vocation''.
{{right|''Barrow'', Sermons, III. xiv.}}}}
='''Syn. 2.''' ''Calling'', ''Business'', etc. See ''occupation.''

'''vocational''' (vọ̄-kā′shọn-ạl), ''a.''   [< ''vocation'' + ''-al.'']   Pertaining or relating to a vocation or occupation.
{{smaller block|Sailors are a class apart, but only in a ''vocational'' sense.
{{right|''Daily Telegraph'', Jan. 2, 1886. (''Encyc. Dict.'')}}}}

'''vocationally''' (vọ̄-kā′shọn-ạl-i), ''adv.'' As respects a vocation, occupation, or trade.
{{smaller block|But the seamanship of those days, the strategies, the devices, the expedients, are no longer of the least value ''vocationally''. {{right|''Athenæum'', No. 3266, p. 697.}}}}

'''vocative''' (vok′a̤-tiv), ''a.'' and ''n.''   [< F. ''vocatif'' = Sp. Pg. It. ''vocativo'' = G. ''vocativ'', < L. ''vocativus'', of or pertaining to calling, as a noun (sc. ''casus'') the vocative case, < ''vocare'', pp. ''vocatus'', call: see ''vocation.'']   '''I.''' ''a.'' Relating to the act of calling or addressing by name; compellative: applied to the grammatical case in which a person or thing is addressed: as, the ''vocative'' case.

'''II.''' ''n.'' In ''gram.'', the case employed in calling to or addressing a person or thing: as, ''Domine'', ‘O Lord,’ is the ''vocative'' of the Latin ''dominus''.

'''Vochysia''' (vō-kis′i-ä̤), ''n.''   [NL. (Jussieu, 1789), from the name among the Galibis of Guiana.]   A genus of plants, type of the order ''Vochysiaceæ.''
{{smaller block|It is characterized by flowers with three (or fewer) petals, a single fertile stamen, and a three-celled ovary with two ovules in each cell. There are about 55 species, natives of Brazil, Guiana, eastern Peru, and the United States of Colombia. They are tall trees, or sometimes shrubs, often resinous, and with very handsomely netted-veined coriaceous leaves. The flowers are large, bright-orange or yellow, and odorous, forming elongated compound racemes or panicles; the leaves are decussate and opposite, or whorled. The wood is a valuable compact but not durable timber; that of ''V. Guianensis'' is known as ''itaballi-wood'' and ''copaiyé-wood.'' The flowers are singularly irregular: the posterior sepal is much larger than the other four, and usually spurred, and the petals are linear and spatulate, the anterior being much the larger. The fruit is a coriaceous and woody three-celled and three-valved capsule, containing three erect winged or cottony seeds.}}

'''Vochysiaceæ''' (vō-kis-i-ā′sē-ē), ''n. pl.''   [NL. (A. St. Hilaire, 1820), < ''Vochysia'' + ''-aceæ.'']   An order of polypetalous plants, of the series ''Thalamifloræ'' and cohort ''Polygalinæ.'' {{smaller|It is characterized by irregular flowers, a three-celled ovary, and a straight embryo, usually without albumen. It includes about 130 species, belonging to 7 genera, of which the type ''Vochysia'' with 55, ''Qualea'' with 33, and ''Trigonia'' with 25 species are the chief; all occur mostly in Brazil and Guiana. They are trees, often of immense size and with a copious resinous juice, fetid in the genus ''Callisthene;'' a few are shrubs, and one genus, ''Trigonia,'' is sarmentose or twining. The flowers are bisexual, irregular, variously colored, often large, handsome, and odorous, and commonly racemose or panicled. They are remarkable in some of the genera for producing but a single petal, or but a single fertile stamen. The fruit is usually an oblong terete or three-angled capsule, with three coriaceous valves, often with winged pilose or cottony seeds, and large leaf-like corrugated cotyledons; in ''Erisma,'' a genus of trees of great size, the fruit is a very peculiar samara with long coriaceous falcate reticulated wings developed from calyx-segments.}}

'''vociferance''' (vō-sif′e-rans), ''n.''   [< ''vociferan(t)'' + ''-ce.'']   Vociferation; clamor; noise.
{{smaller block|All now is wrangle, abuse, and ''vociferance.''
{{right|''Browning,'' Master Hugues of Saxe-Gotha.}}}}

'''vociferant''' (vō-sif′e-rant), ''a.'' and ''n.''   [< L. ''vociferan(t-)s,'' ppr. of ''vociferari,'' cry out: see ''vociferate.'']   '''I.''' ''a.'' Clamorous; noisy; vociferous.
{{smaller block|The most ''vociferant'' vulgar, who most cry up this their Diana, like the riotous rabble at Ephesus, do least know what the matter is.
{{right|''Bp. Gauden,'' Tears of the Church, p. 114. (''Davies.'')}}}}
{{smaller block|That placid flock, that pastor ''vociferant.''
{{right|''Browning,'' Christmas Eve.}}}}

'''II.''' ''n.'' One who is clamorous; one given to vociferation.

{{smaller block|Strange as it may appear to earnest but misguided ''vociferants'', there has been no statutory change in the tenure of the great majority of inferior officers in the civil branch of the executive department. {{right|''The Atlantic'', LXV. 675.}}}}

'''vociferate''' (vō-sif′ẹ-rāt), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''vociferated'', ppr. ''vociferating''.   [< L. ''vociferatus'', pp. of ''vociferari'' (> It. ''vociferare'' = Sp. Pg. ''vociferar'' = F. ''vociférer''), cry out, scream, < ''vox'' (''voc-''), voice, + ''ferre'' = E. ''bear''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''I.''' ''intrans.'' To cry out noisily; make an outcry.
{{smaller block|<poem>So saying, he lash’d the shoulders of his steeds,
And, through the ranks ''vociferating'', call’d
His Trojans on. {{right|''Cowper'', Iliad, xv. 434.}}</poem>}}
{{smaller|='''Syn.''' To shout, bellow, roar, bawl.}}
'''II.''' ''trans.'' To utter with a loud voice; assert or proclaim clamorously; shout.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Vociferated'' logic kills me quite;
A noisy man is always in the right.
{{right|''Cowper'', Conversation, l. 113.}}</poem>}}
{{smaller block|Clamouring all the time against our unfairness, like one who, while changing the cards, diverts the attention of the table from his sleight of hand by ''vociferating'' charges of foul play against other people. {{right|''Macaulay'', Utilitarian Theory of Government.}}}}

'''vociferation''' (vō-sif-ẹ-rā′shọn), ''n.''   [< F. ''vociférations'', pl., = Sp. ''vociferacion'' = Pg. ''vociferação'' = It. ''vociferazione'', < L. ''vociferatio''(''n''-), clamor, outcry, < ''vociferari'', cry out: see ''vociferate''.]   The act of vociferating; noisy exclamation; violent outcry; clamor.
{{smaller block|His excuses were over-ruled by a great majority, and with much ''vociferation''. {{right|''Goldsmith'', Clubs.}}}}
{{smaller block|Distinguished by his violent ''vociferation'', and repeated imprecations upon the king and the conquerors. {{right|''Bruce'', Source of the Nile, II. 333.}}}}

'''vociferator''' (vọ̄-sif′e̤-rā-to̤r), ''n.'' One who vociferates; a clamorous shouter.
{{smaller block|He defied the ''vociferators'' to do their worst.
{{right|''Daily Telegraph'', Oct. 27, 1887. (''Encyc. Dict.'')}}}}

'''vociferize''' (vọ̄-sif′ėr-īz), ''v.'' Same as ''vociferate.''   [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Let the singing singers
With vocal voices, most vociferous
In sweet vociferation, out-''vociferize''
Even sound itself.</poem>
{{right|''Carey'', Chrononhotonthologos, i. 1.}}}}

'''vociferosity''' (vọ̄-sif-e̤-ros′ị-ti), ''n.''   [< ''vociferous'' + ''-ity.'']   The character of being vociferous; vociferation; clamorousness. [Rare.]<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
